scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for a parent to force their 13-year-old son to play sports or join some extracurricular activity because the son is really lazy. The parent is frustrated because the son gets C's in middle school, talks in class, doesn't clean up after himself, and spends a lot of time playing games. The parent also mentions that the son doesn't shower unless told and seems to avoid any kind of productive activity. The mother, who shares custody, isn't helping by enabling this behavior. The parent is considering forcing the son to play basketball for a season to instill some work ethic and discipline. First, I need to understand the parent's perspective. They're worried about their son's future and want to help him develop better habits and a work ethic. They see sports or extracurricular activities as a way to get the son out of his comfort zone and into a structured environment where he can learn teamwork, responsibility, and the value of hard work. On the other hand, forcing a child into an activity they don't want to participate in could have negative consequences. It might lead to resentment, resistance, or even more defiance. The child might feel like they're being controlled or that their autonomy is being taken away, which could harm the parent-child relationship. I also need to consider the child's perspective. At 13, it's a tough age where kids are trying to establish their independence and figure out who they are. Being forced into an activity might make them feel like they're not being heard or respected. It could also lead to stress or anxiety if they're not interested in the activity or feel pressured to perform. Another angle is the effectiveness of forcing versus encouraging. Sometimes, when children are forced into something, they might not engage fully or might not develop the intended skills because they're not genuinely interested. Encouraging them to try new things and supporting their interests might be a better approach. I should also think about alternatives. Maybe instead of forcing the son into sports, the parent could explore other activities that might interest him. It could be something like a hobby, a club, or even a part-time job. The key is to find something that aligns with his interests but still provides structure and opportunities for growth. Communication is another important factor. The parent should have an open and honest conversation with the son about their concerns and why they think joining an extracurricular activity would be beneficial. Understanding the son's reasons for not wanting to participate could help the parent address those specific issues. Setting boundaries and expectations is also crucial. The parent could establish clear rules and consequences for not meeting certain responsibilities, like doing chores or maintaining a certain level of academic performance. This way, the son knows what is expected of him and the consequences of not meeting those expectations. Support and encouragement are key. Instead of forcing, the parent could offer support and encouragement for the son to try new things. This might involve helping him find an activity he's interested in, providing resources, or even participating in the activity with him to make it more enjoyable. I also need to consider the role of the other parent. Since the mother isn't pushing the son to do anything, it might be helpful for the parents to communicate and come up with a united approach to parenting. Consistency is important for children to understand expectations and boundaries. In summary, while the parent's intentions are good—to help the son develop a work ethic and better habits—forcing him into an activity he doesn't want to participate in might not be the most effective approach. It could lead to resentment and resistance. Instead, the parent could focus on open communication, exploring the son's interests, setting clear expectations, and providing support and encouragement to help him develop the necessary skills and work ethic in a way that feels more collaborative and less forced.
